cls: Water-soluble B-vitamin (amide form of niacin / vitamin B3)
pharm: The amide form of niacin (vitamin B3) and a precursor of the coenzymes NAD and NADP that are essential for cellular energy metabolism and redox reactions. Used to prevent and treat niacin (vitamin B3) deficiency / pellagra and, unlike nicotinic acid, it does not cause flushing and does not lower lipids.
quick: Deficiency/pellagra: up to ~500 mg/day in divided doses; RDA ~14-16 mg/day
May be taken with or without food; with food if mild GI upset
Recommended dietary amounts are safe; high doses only if indicated
Recommended dietary amounts are safe and recommended
Use cautiously at high doses; reduced clearance
High doses can rarely cause hepatotoxicity - monitor in liver disease
Alcohol use is a common cause of B3 deficiency; no direct flushing interaction
Resolution of deficiency; LFTs and glucose with high-dose/prolonged use
summary: Niacinamide (nicotinamide) is the amide form of niacin, vitamin B3. It is converted in the body to the coenzymes NAD and NADP, which are central to oxidation-reduction reactions and cellular energy metabolism. It is used to prevent and treat vitamin B3 deficiency and pellagra (dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia). Unlike nicotinic acid (the other form of niacin), niacinamide does NOT cause cutaneous flushing and does NOT have lipid-lowering effects, so it is preferred when only vitamin replacement is needed. The recommended dietary allowance for adults is about 14-16 mg/day (niacin equivalents); therapeutic doses for deficiency are higher (commonly up to about 500 mg/day in divided doses). High doses can, rarely, cause hepatotoxicity and glucose intolerance. It is widely available as a vitamin supplement and is also used topically in dermatology.
indications: Prevention and treatment of niacin (vitamin B3) deficiency and pellagra
Dietary supplementation to meet vitamin B3 requirements (including in malnutrition, alcoholism, malabsorption)

dosage.d: About 14 mg/day (women) to 16 mg/day (men) of niacin equivalents
dosage.n: Higher in pregnancy (~18 mg) and lactation (~17 mg)

dosage.d: Commonly 50-100 mg three to five times daily (up to ~500 mg/day) in divided doses
dosage.n: Continue until clinical recovery; treat associated B-vitamin deficiencies

dosage.d: Parenteral niacinamide where oral therapy is not feasible, per product directions
Per age/weight and product directions (lower than adult therapeutic doses)

admin: Take orally with water; may be taken with or without food, with food if it causes mild stomach upset
Use divided doses for higher therapeutic amounts
Treat coexisting deficiencies (other B vitamins, protein) in pellagra/malnutrition
Reserve high prolonged doses for clear indications and monitor liver function and glucose
moa: Niacinamide is incorporated into the coenzymes nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADP). These coenzymes act as hydrogen/electron carriers in numerous oxidation-reduction reactions essential for tissue respiration, glycolysis, lipid metabolism, and ATP production. Adequate niacinamide therefore prevents and reverses the multisystem manifestations of vitamin B3 deficiency (pellagra). It is also a substrate for poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) and sirtuin pathways. Unlike nicotinic acid, niacinamide does not activate the GPR109A receptor responsible for flushing or affect lipoprotein metabolism, so it neither flushes nor lowers cholesterol/triglycerides.

relative: Active liver disease or unexplained transaminase elevations (hepatotoxicity risk at high doses)
Diabetes mellitus / glucose intolerance (high doses may worsen glycemic control)
Gout/hyperuricemia (high doses, less than with nicotinic acid)
monitor: Liver function tests with high-dose or prolonged therapy
Blood glucose in patients with or at risk of diabetes

preg: Niacinamide in recommended dietary amounts is safe and required in pregnancy (RDA about 18 mg/day of niacin equivalents). High doses should be used only when clearly indicated for a deficiency state.
lact: Niacinamide in recommended dietary amounts is safe and recommended during breastfeeding (RDA about 17 mg/day) and is a normal constituent of breast milk. Avoid unnecessary high-dose supplementation.
renal: Use high doses cautiously in renal impairment because clearance may be reduced; usual dietary/replacement doses do not require adjustment.
hepatic: High doses of niacinamide can rarely cause hepatotoxicity; use cautiously and monitor liver function in patients with hepatic disease. Usual replacement doses are generally well tolerated.

moderate: Antidiabetic agents - high-dose niacinamide may raise blood glucose and reduce glycemic control
Carbamazepine / primidone - niacinamide may increase their plasma levels
minor: Hepatotoxic drugs - theoretical additive risk with high-dose niacinamide
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food.
interactions.alcohol: Chronic alcohol use is a frequent cause of vitamin B3 deficiency; there is no flushing interaction (unlike nicotinic acid + alcohol).
interactions.diagnostics: Generally none; high doses may slightly affect glucose measurements via altered glycemic control.

common: Generally well tolerated at usual doses
Mild nausea or stomach upset at high doses
emergency: Signs of severe hepatotoxicity (jaundice, severe abdominal pain) with very high doses

monitoring: Resolution of deficiency/pellagra signs (skin, GI, neurologic)
Liver function tests with high-dose or prolonged therapy
Blood glucose in diabetic or at-risk patients on high doses
counsel: Niacinamide is a form of vitamin B3 used to prevent or treat vitamin B3 deficiency (pellagra)
Unlike plain niacin, niacinamide does NOT cause flushing or warmth, and it does not lower cholesterol
Take it with water, with or without food; take with food if it upsets your stomach
Very high doses for a long time can affect the liver or blood sugar - take high doses only as advised and keep follow-up blood tests
Eating a balanced diet (meat, fish, eggs, legumes, fortified grains) usually provides enough vitamin B3
Tell your doctor if you have liver disease, diabetes, or are taking seizure medicines
pk: Deficiency symptoms improve within days of replacement
Plasma Tmax within ~1 hour of an oral dose
Water-soluble; excess excreted in urine - dose regularly
Store at room temperature, protected from light and moisture
pearls: Niacinamide is the amide of vitamin B3 - converted to the coenzymes NAD/NADP
Key clinical distinction: niacinamide does NOT flush and does NOT lower lipids, unlike nicotinic acid (niacin)
First-line for treating/preventing pellagra and dietary B3 deficiency
High prolonged doses can cause hepatotoxicity and worsen glycemic control - monitor LFTs and glucose
Water-soluble vitamin available OTC/as a supplement; also used topically in dermatology (acne, rosacea, pigmentation)
missed: If you miss a dose, take it when you remember. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and continue your regular schedule. Do not take a double dose.
overdose: Niacinamide has low acute toxicity because excess is excreted in the urine. Very large doses can cause nausea, vomiting, and, rarely with chronic high intake, hepatotoxicity and impaired glucose tolerance. Treatment is to stop the supplement and provide supportive care; monitor liver function and glucose if very high amounts were taken. Contact a poison control center for large ingestions.
